name: Jetty Prime
geological_features: Archipelago chains extending like jetties from continental shelves
Shallow continental seas rich in dissolved minerals
Basalt plateaus covered in thick loam soils
specific_features: Colonial settlement of approximately 12,000 inhabitants on the largest archipelago
description: Jetty Prime is a medium terrestrial world whose dominant geographical feature is a series of narrow archipelago chains that extend hundreds of kilometers from the continental margins like natural jetties reaching into the sea. The islands are basalt-cored and soil-rich, supporting dense vegetation that ranges from towering canopy forests on the larger islands to salt-tolerant scrubland on the wave-washed outer reaches. The continental interiors are broad plateaus of fertile volcanic soil under temperate skies.

The atmosphere is clean and mild, carrying the scent of ocean salt and the green perfume of vigorous plant life. Winds are steady and moderate, driven by reliable thermal patterns that early colonists quickly learned to predict. The light has a particular quality — warm and golden in the morning, crisp and blue-white at midday — that colonists describe as one of the planet's most immediately welcoming features.

Human settlement on Jetty Prime began forty years ago as a botanical research station studying the planet's remarkably diverse flora, which includes several species producing compounds not found in any known biochemistry. The station grew into a permanent colony as researchers brought families and support staff, and the settlement now functions as a largely self-sufficient agricultural community with a strong scientific focus. The flora has been cooperative — no toxic species have been identified, and several have proved highly nutritious.

Jetty Prime is widely regarded as one of the most successful colonial ventures in the sector, its combination of breathable atmosphere, fertile soil, and benign biology making it an exemplar of what planetary settlement can achieve. Expansion applications are pending for three additional settlement sites along different archipelago chains, though environmental impact assessments are proceeding cautiously to avoid repeating the ecological mistakes of earlier colonial efforts elsewhere.
